broch.name: Broch
broch.summary: An Iron Age drystone hollow-walled roundhouse structure found across Atlantic Scotland, with the earliest examples possibly built around 300 BCE.

ine-of-wessex.name: Ine of Wessex
ine-of-wessex.summary: King of Wessex in southern England from 689 to 726, known for issuing an early written code of Anglo-Saxon laws around 694 and for growing trade during his reign.

hide-unit.name: hide (unit)
hide-unit.summary: An archaic English land measure meant to represent enough land to support a household, used to assess taxes, army service and food-rent obligations, and recorded in the 1086 Domesday Book.

bede.name: Bede
bede.summary: An English Benedictine monk (672/3-735) called the 'Father of English History' for his Ecclesiastical History of the English People, and a noted scholar of scripture and calendars.

anglesey.name: Anglesey
anglesey.summary: An island off the northwest coast of Wales, the largest island in Wales, and a heartland of the Welsh language.

tribal-hidage.name: Tribal Hidage
tribal-hidage.summary: A list of thirty-five tribes and territories in Anglo-Saxon England, compiled between the 7th and 9th centuries, assigning each a number of hides, possibly for tribute purposes.

beowulf.name: Beowulf
beowulf.summary: An Old English epic poem of 3,182 lines about a Geatish hero who defeats the monster Grendel and, decades later, a dragon; the surviving manuscript dates to 975–1025.

picts.name: Picts
picts.summary: A group of peoples living in what is now Scotland north of the Firth of Forth during the Early Middle Ages, whose name may derive from the Latin word for 'painted'.

insular-art.name: Insular art
insular-art.summary: Also called Hiberno-Saxon art, a style produced in post-Roman Britain and Ireland from around 600, known for interlace decoration in illuminated manuscripts and metalwork, ended by Viking raids from the late 8th century.

book-of-kells.name: Book of Kells
book-of-kells.summary: An illustrated Latin Gospel manuscript made around 800 AD in a Columban monastery in Ireland or Scotland, regarded as the pinnacle of Insular art.

iona.name: Iona
iona.summary: A small island in Scotland's Inner Hebrides, home to Iona Abbey and known as the birthplace of Celtic Christianity in Scotland since St Columba founded a monastery there in 563.

cluny-abbey.name: Cluny Abbey
cluny-abbey.summary: A Benedictine monastery in France founded in 910 that led a movement of reform across Western European monasteries and became the leader of western monasticism.

first-romanesque.name: First Romanesque
first-romanesque.summary: Early style of Romanesque architecture from the 10th to early 11th century, originating in Lombardy, marked by thick walls, plain facades, and rhythmic blind arches called Lombard bands.

d-l-riata.name: Dál Riata
d-l-riata.summary: A Gaelic kingdom spanning western Scotland and northeastern Ireland, at its height in the 6th–7th centuries, home to the influential monastery of Iona and a strong seafaring culture.

northumbria.name: Northumbria
northumbria.summary: An early medieval English kingdom existing from 654 to 1066 AD, spanning modern northern England and southern Scotland at its height.

franks-casket.name: Franks Casket
franks-casket.summary: Small Anglo-Saxon whalebone chest from the early 8th century, densely carved with runic inscriptions mixing Christian, Roman and Germanic legend; now in the British Museum.

sutton-hoo.name: Sutton Hoo
sutton-hoo.summary: Site in Suffolk, England of Anglo-Saxon cemeteries from the 6th-7th centuries, famous for a 1938 ship burial with gold, gems, a helmet and other treasures that illuminate a poorly documented era.

carolingian-art.name: Carolingian art
carolingian-art.summary: Art produced in the Frankish Empire from about 780 to 900 under Charlemagne and his heirs, blending classical Mediterranean styles with Northern traditions and paving the way for Romanesque art.

ripon.name: Ripon
ripon.summary: A small cathedral city in North Yorkshire, England, whose history traces back to an early Anglo-Saxon monastery and which later became known for wool, cloth and spur-making.

hexham-abbey.name: Hexham Abbey
hexham-abbey.summary: A church in Northumberland, England, originally built in 674 and rebuilt into its current form in the 12th century, serving as the town's parish church since the monasteries' dissolution in 1537.

dalmeny.name: Dalmeny
dalmeny.summary: A village in Scotland near Edinburgh where Scotland's only known pagan burial was found, containing a necklace and a gold filigree object resembling finds at Sutton Hoo.

thelstan.name: Æthelstan
thelstan.summary: King of the Anglo-Saxons from 924 and King of the English from 927 until his death in 939, regarded as the first King of England; he defeated a Viking-Scottish alliance at Brunanburh in 937.

olaf-guthfrithson.name: Olaf Guthfrithson
olaf-guthfrithson.summary: A Hiberno-Scandinavian king of Dublin and Viking Northumbria who died in 941, allied with Scotland against England but was defeated at the Battle of Brunanburh in 937.

constantine-ii-of-scotland.name: Constantine II of Scotland
constantine-ii-of-scotland.summary: An early King of Scotland (Alba) (born no later than 879 – died 952), whose reign was dominated by conflicts with Norse rulers and English kings like Æthelstan.

battle-of-brunanburh.name: Battle of Brunanburh
battle-of-brunanburh.summary: A battle fought in 937 in which King Æthelstan of England defeated an invading alliance of the kings of Dublin, Scotland and Strathclyde, seen by some historians as shaping the political map of the British Isles.

fyrd.name: Fyrd
fyrd.summary: An early Anglo-Saxon military force raised from freemen or paid men, reorganized under Alfred the Great alongside a network of fortified towns called burhs to defend against Viking raids.

offa-of-mercia.name: Offa of Mercia
offa-of-mercia.summary: King of Mercia from 757 to 796 who extended Anglo-Saxon Mercian power over most of southern England and clashed with the Church over ecclesiastical authority.

mercia.name: Mercia
mercia.summary: An early medieval Anglo-Saxon kingdom centered on the River Trent in the English Midlands, dominant over southern England during its 'Golden Age' from about 600 to 900.

alfred-the-great.name: Alfred the Great
alfred-the-great.summary: King of the West Saxons from 871 and King of the Anglo-Saxons from 886 until 899, who defeated the Vikings at the Battle of Edington in 878 and later retook London from them.

anglo-saxon-chronicle.name: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
anglo-saxon-chronicle.summary: A set of Old English annals on Anglo-Saxon history, first compiled in the late 800s under King Alfred the Great and copied and updated at English monasteries until 1154; its oldest surviving manuscript, held at Cambridge, is called the Parker Chronicle.

penda-of-mercia.name: Penda
penda-of-mercia.summary: A 7th-century pagan king of Mercia (died 655) who defeated several rival Anglo-Saxon rulers, laying the foundations for Mercian dominance before being killed in battle.

shield-wall.name: Shield wall
shield-wall.summary: A military formation common in ancient and medieval warfare in which soldiers stood shoulder to shoulder with overlapping shields for mutual protection.

kincardineshire.name: Kincardineshire
kincardineshire.summary: A historic county, also called the Mearns, on the northeast coast of Scotland, which functioned as an administrative area until 1975.

caithness.name: Caithness
caithness.summary: A historic county in the far north of mainland Scotland, ruled from the 9th century by the Jarl of Orkney before becoming a separate earldom in the 14th century.

john-of-worcester.name: John of Worcester
john-of-worcester.summary: English monk and chronicler at Worcester Priory (died c. 1140), usually held to be the author of the Chronicon ex Chronicis.

thelweard-historian.name: Æthelweard
thelweard-historian.summary: English ealdorman who died around 998 and wrote a Latin version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, known as the Chronicon Æthelweardi.

bromborough.name: Bromborough
bromborough.summary: Town on the Wirral Peninsula in Merseyside, England, generally agreed to be the site of a great battle referred to in early medieval chronicles.

wirral-peninsula.name: Wirral Peninsula
wirral-peninsula.summary: Peninsula in North West England bounded by the Dee Estuary, the Mersey Estuary and Liverpool Bay, historically part of Cheshire.

sequence-of-saint-eulalia.name: Sequence of Saint Eulalia
sequence-of-saint-eulalia.summary: The earliest surviving piece of French hagiography, composed in verse around 880, recounting the martyrdom of Eulalia of Mérida.

widsith.name: Widsith
widsith.summary: An Old English poem of 143 lines surviving in the 10th-century Exeter Book, surveying kings and heroes of the Heroic Age of Northern Europe.

exeter-book.name: Exeter Book
exeter-book.summary: A late-10th-century manuscript of Old English poetry, the largest surviving collection of its kind, given to Exeter Cathedral in 1072 and recognized by UNESCO in 2016.

attila.name: Attila
attila.summary: Ruler of the Huns from 434 until his death in 453, known as "the Scourge of God," who invaded the Balkans, Gaul and Italy but never took Rome or Constantinople.

ermanaric.name: Ermanaric
ermanaric.summary: Greuthungian Gothic king who died in 376, said by some ancient and later legendary sources to have ruled a vast realm before the Hunnic invasion.

hl-skvi-a.name: Battle of the Goths and Huns
hl-skvi-a.summary: The English name for Hlöðskviða, an Old Norse heroic poem found in the Hervarar saga that fictionalizes a battle, likely set in the 4th or 5th century, between Goths and Huns.

boethius.name: Boethius
boethius.summary: Roman senator, consul and philosopher (c. 480–524 CE) who translated Greek classics into Latin, becoming a central bridge between Classical and Christian scholarship.

on-the-consolation-of-philosophy.name: The Consolation of Philosophy
on-the-consolation-of-philosophy.summary: Philosophical work written by Boethius in 523 while imprisoned and awaiting execution, often called the last great Western work of the Classical Period.

carolingian-renaissance.name: Carolingian Renaissance
carolingian-renaissance.summary: A revival of learning, writing, and the arts in the Carolingian Empire under Charlemagne and his successors, drawing inspiration from ancient Roman, Greek, and Christian culture.

alcuin.name: Alcuin of York
alcuin.summary: Anglo-Saxon scholar and teacher (c. 735–804) from York who led Charlemagne's court school and helped shape the Carolingian Renaissance.

lotte-hedeager.name: Lotte Hedeager
lotte-hedeager.summary: A Danish archaeologist, born 1948, who is a professor of archaeology at the University of Oslo.

john-niles-scholar.name: John Niles
john-niles-scholar.summary: American scholar (born 1945) of medieval English literature, best known for his work on Beowulf and the theory of oral literature.

ecclesiastical-history-of-the-english-pe.name: Ecclesiastical History of the English People
ecclesiastical-history-of-the-english-pe.summary: A history of Christianity in England written in Latin by Bede around 731 CE, considered one of the most important original sources on Anglo-Saxon history.
ecclesiastical-history-of-the-english-pe.source_title: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

canu-heledd.name: Canu Heledd
canu-heledd.summary: A collection of early Welsh poems, unusual for being voiced by a female character, centered on the death of her brother Cynddylan.

cynddylan.name: Cynddylan
cynddylan.summary: Seventh-century Prince of Powys, known only from later literary sources such as the poem Marwnad Cynddylan (Elegy for Cynddylan), with no other historical record of his reign.

pengwern.name: Pengwern
pengwern.summary: A Brythonic settlement of sub-Roman Britain in what is now Shropshire, possibly an early seat of the kings of Powys.

dogfeiling.name: Dogfeiling
dogfeiling.summary: A minor sub-kingdom, later a commote, on the eastern border of Gwynedd in early medieval Wales, existing from 445 until about 700.

newtown-powys.name: Newtown, Powys
newtown-powys.summary: A market town in Powys, Wales, on the River Severn; the largest town in Mid Wales and birthplace of social reformer Robert Owen in 1771.

hervarar-saga-ok-hei-reks.name: Hervarar saga ok Heiðreks
hervarar-saga-ok-hei-reks.summary: A 13th-century legendary Norse saga combining older Germanic heroic tales of wars between Goths and Huns, including poetic sections on the sword Tyrfing and their great battle.

gesta-danorum.name: Gesta Danorum
gesta-danorum.summary: 12th-century Latin chronicle by Saxo Grammaticus covering Danish and Scandinavian history from prehistory to the late 1100s, and an early source for Estonia and Latvia too.

bald-s-leechbook.name: Bald's Leechbook
bald-s-leechbook.summary: A medical text in Old English and Latin, likely compiled in the mid-10th century and named after its owner, Bald; survives in one British Library manuscript alongside a related text, Leechbook III.

the-reckoning-of-time.name: The Reckoning of Time
the-reckoning-of-time.summary: Latin treatise written by the Northumbrian monk Bede in 725, describing ancient calendars and chiefly focused on calculating the date of Easter.

charlemagne.name: Charlemagne
charlemagne.summary: King of the Franks from 768 and emperor of the Carolingian Empire from 800, who united most of Western and Central Europe and was the first recognised western emperor since Rome's fall.

york-minster.name: York Minster
york-minster.summary: An Anglican cathedral in York, seat of the Archbishop of York, built mainly between 1220 and 1472 and famed for its medieval stained glass.

pope-sylvester-ii.name: Pope Sylvester II (Gerbert of Aurillac)
pope-sylvester-ii.summary: Scholar-pope who led the Papal States from 999 to 1003 and reintroduced the abacus, armillary sphere and Hindu-Arabic decimal numerals to Western Christendom.

al-andalus.name: Al-Andalus
al-andalus.summary: The Muslim-ruled territories of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 to 1492, which at their height covered all of Spain and Portugal, with Córdoba becoming a leading cultural and scientific center.

dionysius-exiguus.name: Dionysius Exiguus
dionysius-exiguus.summary: 6th-century Eastern Roman monk best known as the inventor of Anno Domini (AD) dating, still used to number years in the Gregorian and Julian calendars.

date-of-easter.name: Computus
date-of-easter.summary: The traditional calculation used to fix the date of Easter each year, aligning lunar months with the solar calendar and the March equinox.

lacnunga.name: Lacnunga
lacnunga.summary: A collection of Anglo-Saxon medical texts and prayers in Old English and Latin, compiled in England around the late 10th or early 11th century.

atto-bishop-of-vic.name: Atto of Vic
atto-bishop-of-vic.summary: Bishop of Vic from 957 until 971, who had the bishopric raised to an archbishopric but was assassinated by his opponents.

richerus.name: Richer
richerus.summary: A 10th-century monk at Saint-Remi near Reims and historian, an important source for the contemporary kingdom of France.

wessex.name: Wessex
wessex.summary: The Anglo-Saxon Kingdom of the West Saxons in southern Great Britain, from around 519 to 927, whose rulers eventually united England under one crown.

cnut.name: Cnut
cnut.summary: King of England from 1016, Denmark from 1018, and Norway from 1028 until his death in 1035, ruling the three kingdoms together as the North Sea Empire.

north-sea-empire.name: North Sea Empire
north-sea-empire.summary: Personal union of England, Denmark and Norway under Norse kings for most of 1013 to 1042; at its height under Cnut the Great it was the most powerful realm in western Europe after the Holy Roman Empire.

great-heathen-army.name: Great Heathen Army
great-heathen-army.summary: Old English for the Great Army, a coalition of mostly Danish Viking warriors who invaded England in 865 aiming to conquer its four kingdoms, led by sons of Ragnar Lodbrok.

west-francia.name: West Francia
west-francia.summary: The West Frankish kingdom formed from the 843 division of the Carolingian Empire, lasting until 987 and evolving into the Kingdom of France under the Capetian dynasty.

capetian-dynasty.name: Capetian dynasty
capetian-dynasty.summary: A royal dynasty of Frankish origin founded by Hugh Capet in 987, whose male line and later Valois and Bourbon branches ruled France almost continuously into the 19th century.

offa-s-dyke.name: Offa's Dyke
offa-s-dyke.summary: A large earthwork roughly following the England–Wales border, traditionally credited to King Offa of Mercia, though evidence points to earlier origins.

witan.name: Witan
witan.summary: The king's council in Anglo-Saxon England from before the 7th century to the 11th century, made up of noblemen who advised on legislation and other national matters.

ealdorman.name: Ealdorman
ealdorman.summary: A high office in the government of Anglo-Saxon England, which by the 11th century had evolved into the title of earl.

thegn.name: Thegn
thegn.summary: An aristocratic rank in later Anglo-Saxon England, ranking below the king and ealdormen and requiring substantial landownership; roughly equivalent to a modern baron.

hywel-dda.name: Hywel Dda
hywel-dda.summary: A Welsh king who died around 950 and came to rule most of Wales, remembered for codifying Welsh law in the Laws of Hywel Dda.

deheubarth.name: Deheubarth
deheubarth.summary: A historical name for the kingdoms of south Wales, used to distinguish them from Gwynedd in the north; it was a loose grouping of southern Welsh territories rather than a single formal realm.

idwal-foel.name: Idwal Foel
idwal-foel.summary: A 10th-century King of Gwynedd in Wales (died c. 942), a member of the House of Aberffraw who inherited the throne from his father Anarawd ap Rhodri.

gwynedd.name: Gwynedd
gwynedd.summary: A mountainous county in north-west Wales, home to much of Snowdonia and a heartland of the Welsh language.

edmund-i.name: Edmund I
edmund-i.summary: King of the English from 939 to 946, grandson of Alfred the Great, who recovered territory lost to Viking rulers before being killed in a brawl at age 25.

house-of-alpin.name: House of Alpin
house-of-alpin.summary: A kin-group that ruled Pictland and the kingdom of Alba from the 940s until 1034, tracing its descent from Kenneth MacAlpin, who united the Scots and Picts.

dumbarton-castle.name: Alt Clut
dumbarton-castle.summary: Welsh name for Dumbarton Rock, stronghold of the Britons of Alt Clut, said to have the longest recorded history of any fortress in Scotland.

bernicia.name: Bernicia
bernicia.summary: Anglo-Saxon kingdom established by Anglian settlers in the 6th century, covering roughly what is now northeastern England and southeastern Scotland; it merged with Deira in the early 7th century to form Northumbria.

harthacnut.name: Harthacnut
harthacnut.summary: King of Denmark from 1035 and King of England from 1040 until his death in 1042, son of Cnut the Great, and the last Dane to rule England.

nidaros.name: Nidaros
nidaros.summary: Medieval name for Trondheim, capital of Norway's first Christian kings and home to the shrine of Saint Olaf, a major pilgrimage site.

housecarl.name: Housecarl
housecarl.summary: A well-trained, salaried household bodyguard used in medieval Scandinavia and, from the 11th century, Anglo-Saxon England, including at the Battle of Hastings.

aachen.name: Aachen
aachen.summary: A German city near the Belgian and Dutch borders that became the main royal residence of the Frankish Empire under Charlemagne around 800 CE and the coronation site of 31 Holy Roman Emperors.

candidus-fl-793-802.name: Candidus
candidus-fl-793-802.summary: An Anglo-Saxon scholar and disciple of Alcuin who served at Charlemagne's court, becoming master of the palace school in 796 and tutor to two of Charlemagne's female relatives.

peter-of-pisa.name: Peter of Pisa
peter-of-pisa.summary: Italian grammarian, deacon and poet (744–799) summoned to Charlemagne's court in 776, where he served as the emperor's primary Latin teacher.

scholasticism.name: Scholasticism
scholasticism.summary: Medieval European method of philosophical and theological study, dominant from about 1100 to 1700, using rigorous logical debate to reconcile Aristotle's philosophy with Christian theology.

john-scotus-eriugena.name: John Scotus Eriugena
john-scotus-eriugena.summary: Irish Neoplatonist philosopher, theologian and poet (c.800–877), called the most original philosopher of the Carolingian era, known for his work Periphyseon.

palace-school.name: Palace School
palace-school.summary: A school within Istanbul's Topkapı Palace that educated enslaved young men and women for the Ottoman administrative elite, teaching law, religion, music and other skills.

pseudo-dionysius-the-areopagite.name: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite
pseudo-dionysius-the-areopagite.summary: Pseudonym of a Syrian or Greek monk and Neoplatonic theologian writing around 485 to 528 AD, who claimed to be a 1st-century disciple of Paul the Apostle; his mystical theology later shaped Christian thought.

fleury-abbey.name: Fleury Abbey
fleury-abbey.summary: A Benedictine monastery founded around 640 near Orléans, France, famous for holding the relics of St. Benedict and for its influential library and school.

theodulf-of-orl-ans.name: Theodulf of Orléans
theodulf-of-orl-ans.summary: Writer, poet and Bishop of Orléans (c. 798–818) under Charlemagne, and likely author of the Libri Carolini, a major statement on religious art in the Middle Ages.

orl-ans.name: Orléans
orl-ans.summary: A city on the Loire in north-central France, capital of the Kingdom of France under the Merovingians and site of the pivotal 1429 siege lifted with Joan of Arc's help during the Hundred Years' War.

paulinus-of-york.name: Paulinus
paulinus-of-york.summary: A Roman missionary who became the first Bishop of York, converting King Edwin of Northumbria to Christianity; later named Archbishop of York by pallium, though too late to take effect, and canonized after his death in 644.

york.name: York
york.summary: A cathedral city in North Yorkshire, England, founded as the Roman Eboracum in AD 71, later capital of Deira, Northumbria and Scandinavian York.

catharism.name: Catharism
catharism.summary: A Christian dualist movement in southern France and northern Italy between the 12th and 14th centuries, branded heretical and crushed by the Albigensian Crusade and Inquisition.

languedoc.name: Languedoc
languedoc.summary: A former province of southern France, with Toulouse as its capital, now largely part of the Occitanie region.

cappadocian-fathers.name: Cappadocian Fathers
cappadocian-fathers.summary: Three Byzantine Christian bishops and theologians of the 4th century -- Basil the Great, Gregory of Nyssa and Gregory of Nazianzus -- who advanced doctrines such as the Trinity, aided by their sister Macrina.

paschasius-radbertus.name: Paschasius Radbertus
paschasius-radbertus.summary: A Carolingian theologian and abbot of Corbie monastery, best known for his 831 treatise on the Eucharist, later canonized in 1073.

lindisfarne.name: Lindisfarne
lindisfarne.summary: A tidal island off north-east England, also called Holy Island, home to an important early monastery under Celtic Christian saints before Viking raids destroyed it.

lindisfarne-gospels.name: Lindisfarne Gospels
lindisfarne-gospels.summary: An illuminated Latin gospel manuscript made around 715–720 at Lindisfarne monastery, considered one of the finest works of Hiberno-Saxon Insular art, now in the British Library.

lupus-servatus.name: Lupus of Ferrières
lupus-servatus.summary: A Benedictine monk and abbot of Ferrières Abbey (c. 805-862) at Charles the Bald's Carolingian court, sometimes called the first humanist of the Early Middle Ages for his scholarship.

abbo-of-fleury.name: Abbo of Fleury
abbo-of-fleury.summary: A monk and abbot of Fleury Abbey near Orléans, France, who lived from about 945 to 1004.

pope-gregory-i.name: Pope Gregory I
pope-gregory-i.summary: Bishop of Rome from 590 to 604, known as Gregory the Great; a former Roman senator's son whose missionaries helped convert Anglo-Saxon England.

gregorian-mission.name: Gregorian mission
gregorian-mission.summary: A Christian mission sent by Pope Gregory the Great to England in 596, led by Augustine of Canterbury, which had established Christianity among the southern Anglo-Saxons by the last missionary's death in 653.

thelberht-of-kent.name: Æthelberht of Kent
thelberht-of-kent.summary: King of Kent from about 589 until his death in 616, and the first Anglo-Saxon king to convert to Christianity, after marrying the Christian Frankish princess Bertha.

augustine-of-canterbury.name: Augustine of Canterbury
augustine-of-canterbury.summary: Christian monk sent by Pope Gregory I in 595 to convert King Æthelberht of Kent, becoming the first Archbishop of Canterbury in 597.

archbishop-of-canterbury.name: Archbishop of Canterbury
archbishop-of-canterbury.summary: The senior bishop of the Church of England and ceremonial head of the worldwide Anglican Communion; the first, Augustine, arrived in England in 597 under Pope Gregory the Great.

danelaw.name: Danelaw
danelaw.summary: The part of England under Danish law from the late 9th century to the Norman Conquest, set up after Viking conquest and defined in treaties following Alfred the Great's victory over Guthrum.

gosforth-cross.name: Gosforth Cross
gosforth-cross.summary: A tall 10th-century Viking stone cross in Cumbria, England, notable for combining Christian and Norse pagan imagery.

ragnar-k.name: Ragnarök
ragnar-k.summary: In Norse mythology, a foretold battle in which major gods including Odin, Thor and Loki perish amid catastrophic disasters, after which the world is reborn and two human survivors repopulate it.

columba.name: Columba
columba.summary: An Irish abbot and missionary (521–597) who founded Iona Abbey in Scotland around 563, spreading Christianity among the Picts and venerated by the Gaels of Dál Riata.

blickling-homilies.name: Blickling homilies
blickling-homilies.summary: A collection of anonymous Old English sermons written down before the end of the 10th century, among the oldest surviving sermon collections from medieval England.

lfric-of-eynsham.name: Ælfric of Eynsham
lfric-of-eynsham.summary: English abbot (about 955 to about 1010) and a highly prolific writer of Old English hagiography, homilies and biblical commentaries.

plainsong.name: Plainsong
plainsong.summary: A body of monophonic chants used in Western Christian liturgy, the exclusive form of church music until polyphony emerged in the ninth century.

mary-magdalene.name: Mary Magdalene
mary-magdalene.summary: A follower of Jesus described in the gospels as present at his crucifixion and resurrection; a 591 sermon by Pope Gregory I later cast her, without biblical basis, as a repentant prostitute.

valkyrie.name: Valkyrie
valkyrie.summary: In Norse mythology, a female figure who guides slain warriors to Odin's hall Valhalla, sometimes appearing as a hero's lover in later sagas and poems.
